chunks.title: Acute red eye: who needs urgent review
chunks.tldr: Most red eyes are benign (conjunctivitis, subconj haemorrhage, blepharitis). Red flags: recent intraocular surgery (endophthalmitis), contact lens (keratitis), corneal graft (rejection), past uveitis/scleritis or AS/RA, septic or ICU patient with lines (endogenous endophthalmitis), SJS/TEN. Pain (not discomfort) or reduced vision rules out simple conjunctivitis. Nausea/vomiting → very high IOP. Boring night pain → scleritis. Photophobia → keratitis/iritis.
points: Redness pattern: circumcorneal (ciliary flush) = intraocular; diffuse tarsal + bulbar = conjunctivitis; sectoral = episcleritis; violaceous = scleritis; lid margins = blepharitis.
Any corneal opacity, ulcer or diffuse haze (± mid-dilated pupil = angle closure) → emergency.
Small pupil = iritis; hypopyon = keratitis, endophthalmitis or iritis → emergency.
chunks.hook: Pain, poor vision or a bad cornea = not conjunctivitis.

chunks.title: Red eye: management principles
chunks.tldr: Neonatal conjunctivitis: chlamydia, gonococcus (systemic therapy) or HSV (risk of encephalitis → admit, IV antiviral). Gonococcal at any age: Gram stain + culture, IV/IM ceftriaxone. HZO: systemic antiviral within 72 h of rash; Hutchinson sign (nose tip) or lid margin lesions predict eye involvement. Keratitis: find the infection (CL, surface disease, anaesthesia, exposure). Uveitis: exclude infection, especially posterior involvement or recent surgery. Never start steroids without ophthalmic assessment. Scleritis: oral NSAIDs first-line. Acute angle closure: IV/oral acetazolamide + topicals + steroid + pilocarpine → laser PI both eyes.

chunks.title: Acute orbital disease
chunks.tldr: Orbital cellulitis: usually children, from ethmoid sinus — fever, pain, lid swelling, proptosis, restricted movements, leucocytosis. Preseptal: no proptosis/motility limit (may be early orbital). Teens: frontoethmoidal spread (intracranial risk). Diabetic/immunocompromised: mucormycosis (high mortality). Mimics: acute Graves (exposure, optic nerve compression), pseudotumour, carotid–cavernous fistula. Optic nerve compromise: poor colour, RAPD. Non-axial proptosis → abscess.
points: Orbital cellulitis is clinical → IV antibiotics immediately; ophthalmology + ENT.
CT (or MRI) for suspected abscess/complications and to separate Graves, pseudotumour, CCF; orbital Doppler for CCF.
Complications: cavernous sinus thrombosis, intracranial abscess (frontal sinus).
chunks.hook: Proptosis + painful restricted eye in a febrile child = orbital cellulitis → IV antibiotics now.

cards.q: What sign distinguishes orbital from preseptal cellulitis?
cards.a: Proptosis and/or restricted (painful) eye movements (± RAPD).

chunks.title: Acute painless visual loss
chunks.tldr: First: one eye or both? (cover each eye) — monocular = globe/optic nerve; bilateral or homonymous = chiasm or behind. Is it truly new? Floaters + flashes + rising curtain = RD (macula on → emergency). Sudden floaters = VH (tear, PDR, RVO). ≥55 with central loss/distortion = wet AMD until proven otherwise. Abrupt = arterial; full recovery = embolus. ≥55 with arterial event → ESR/CRP for GCA. Fundus: no red reflex (VH/RD), widespread/sectoral haemorrhages (CRVO/BRVO), white retina + cherry-red spot (CRAO), disc swelling (AION).
points: Amaurosis fugax → carotid + cardiac work-up; carotid revascularisation if ≥70% stenosis.
No proven acute treatment for RVO, CRAO or NAION — but untreated GCA → rapid bilateral blindness.
GCA fundus can be normal (choroidal ischaemia, posterior ION).
chunks.hook: Old person, sudden loss: think GCA first — bloods today.

chunks.title: Painful visual loss with a white eye
chunks.tldr: Demyelinating optic neuritis: subacute monocular loss, pain on eye movement, colour loss, RAPD, disc normal (⅔) — usually recovers; key is excluding other causes. Pituitary apoplexy: thunderclap headache, uni/bilateral loss, ophthalmoplegia, adrenal crisis → IV hydrocortisone before imaging, urgent neurosurgery. Sphenoid sinusitis: vertex headache + optic neuropathy → drainage + antibiotics. Posterior scleritis: proptosis, choroidal folds, exudative RD, disc swelling; ultrasound best; NSAIDs/steroids.
chunks.hook: Headache + vision loss + collapse = apoplexy → hydrocortisone first.

cards.q: First treatment in suspected pituitary apoplexy?
cards.a: IV hydrocortisone (before imaging), then urgent neurosurgical review.

chunks.title: Double vision, pupils & swollen discs
chunks.tldr: Monocular diplopia = refractive, lens, macula — not intracranial. Binocular: worrying if multiple cranial nerves, neuro signs, severe headache, systemic illness, or age <50. III palsy with pupil involvement or pain = PComm aneurysm → emergency imaging. Microvascular palsies (>50) recover; exclude GCA. INO = MLF; horizontal gaze palsy = pons; vertical = midbrain; fatigable = myasthenia (check breathing/swallowing). Pupils: isolated fixed dilated pupil in a well person = tonic (dilute pilocarpine 0.125% constricts) or pharmacological (no response to 2%). Painful Horner → carotid dissection. Bilateral disc swelling → urgent imaging + check BP (malignant HTN — lower gradually).
points: Decompensated long-standing palsy (e.g. congenital IV) → prisms, often no imaging.
Dilated pupil + reduced consciousness = tentorial herniation.
Light–near dissociation: syphilis or dorsal midbrain (pineal, hydrocephalus).
Pseudopapilloedema: drusen, crowded discs, myelinated fibres.
